one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban argues for extending the Frivaldo doctrine to Sen. Grace Poe's natural-born citizenship case. He has always believed that doubts on legal issues involving elections and popular sovereignty should be resolved in favor of letting our people decide through the ballot -- whenever possible, election issues (not involving crimes or obvious violations) should be settled by voters, not judges and lawyers. A case in point is Frivaldo v. Comelec (June 28, 1996). Juan Frivaldo was overwhelmingly voted governor of Sorsogon by a wide margin of 27,000 votes in 1988 and 57,000 in 1992, but was twice ousted by the SC for having lost his Philippine citizenship in 1983 when naturalized as American. Undaunted, he ran and won again as governor by 20,000 votes in 1995. Again his victory was challenged by the same candidate he defeated; this time Frivaldo claimed to have reacquired Philippine citizenship under RA 7160 by taking his oath of allegiance at 2 PM on June 30, 1995, the day he assumed office. Raul Lee, his opponent, argued Frivaldo was twice ruled an alien and should have possessed citizenship on the last day for COC filing -- or at the latest on the May 8, 1995 election day -- not on the June 30 assumption date; Lee also attacked the haste in processing the repatriation because Frivaldo filed his application only on the day prior, June 29, 1995. The case was assigned to CJ as a new SC associate justice just after his 1995 assumption -- 'the decision I had the honor of writing for the Court upheld Frivaldo's election.' The Court ruled that 'decisions declaring the acquisition or denial of citizenship cannot govern a person's future status with finality ... because a person may subsequently reacquire, or for that matter lose, his citizenship under any of the modes recognized by law'; the two earlier ousters did not bind Frivaldo's current status. Noting the law did not specify when a candidate must possess citizenship, the Court held it sufficient that Frivaldo became a citizen at assumption of office, not necessarily at COC filing or campaign period. Underlying this liberality is CJ's basic legal philosophy upholding popular sovereignty: 'At balance, the question really boils down to a choice of philosophy and perception of how to interpret and apply laws relating to elections: literal or liberal; the letter or the spirit; the naked provision or its ultimate purpose; legal syllogism or substantial justice; in isolation or in the context of social conditions; harshly against or gently in favor of the voters' obvious choice. In applying election laws, it would be far better to err in favor of popular sovereignty than to be right in complex but little understood legalisms.' Noteworthy too is Justice (later CJ) Reynato S. Puno's concurring opinion: 'I concur in the path-breaking ponencia of Mr. Justice Panganiban which is pro-people and pierces the myopia of legalism ... In cases where the sovereign will of the people is at stake, we must not only be legally right, but also politically correct. We cannot fail by making the people succeed.' The issue in Frivaldo's case was his total lack of citizenship, while in Poe's it is merely her alleged lack of natural-born status -- most critics concede her naturalized citizenship. With far more reasons, therefore, the Constitution and laws governing her case should be more liberally construed by letting the 50 million Filipino voters decide. An even better way of removing doubts is the DNA test. For many years the SC was not convinced of DNA testing's legal viability, but starting with Tijing v. CA (March 8, 2001) and People v. Vallejo (May 9, 2002) the Court changed its mind. In Herrera v. Alba (June 15, 2005), 'the Court moved from the issue of according official recognition to DNA analysis as evidence to the issue of observance of procedures in conducting DNA analysis.' Thereafter, the Court issued on Oct 2, 2007 (to take effect Oct 15, 2007) the Rule on DNA Evidence formally laying down procedural protocols. Poe was reported by her lawyer George Garcia to have undergone a DNA matching test to answer her personal quest of 'Who am I?'; to be legally acceptable, the test must be done pursuant to the Rule's protocols. If her biological father, as shown by the DNA test, was a Filipino at the time of her birth, then she is unquestionably a natural-born citizen.
